bp.name: British Parliamentary (BP)
bp.summary: In British Parliamentary debate, there are 4 teams and 8 speakers. Two teams share the Government side and two share the Opposition side, but every team is judged and ranked independently.

Rebuts the Opening Opposition.

qanda.title: Points of Information (POIs) — the Q&A of BP
qanda.explanation: A POI is a short interjection offered by the opposing bench during a speaker's speech. The speaker in control of the floor may accept it and respond, or decline it and continue.
rules: Open from the 1-minute mark to the 6-minute mark of each 7-minute speech — the first and last minute are "protected" and no POIs are allowed.
Each POI should take no more than 15 seconds to offer.
The speaker decides whether to accept or decline — declining is completely acceptable, but engaging with one or two sharp POIs can strengthen a speech.
POIs are not offered during Whip speeches (Government Whip and Opposition Whip).

keyConcepts: Opening teams build the foundation of the debate.
Closing teams must provide a meaningful extension, not repeat earlier arguments.
Whip speakers summarize, weigh, and compare arguments rather than introducing new ones.
Teams are ranked 1st to 4th (not simply Government vs Opposition) — judges decide which team contributed the most to the debate.

asian.name: Asian Parliamentary (AP)
asian.summary: In Asian Parliamentary debate, there are 2 teams — Government and Opposition — with 3 speakers per team (6 speakers total).

Rebuts the Government's arguments.
Rebuilds the Opposition case.
Adds further supporting arguments.

qanda.title: Points of Information (POIs) — the Q&A of AP
qanda.explanation: As in BP, a POI is a short interjection offered by the opposing side during a speaker's speech, which the speaker may accept or decline.
rules: POIs are offered during substantive speeches (PM, DPM, LO, DLO) but NOT during Whip speeches (GW, OW).
Each POI should take no more than 15 seconds; the speaker may accept or decline.
Exact timing and rules can vary slightly by tournament — always check the specific tournament's guidelines.

keyConcepts: The Prime Minister defines the motion and sets the framework for the whole debate.
Deputy speakers rebut the other side while rebuilding and extending their own team's case.
Whip speakers summarize and weigh the debate — they must not raise new substantive arguments.
Unlike BP, there are only two teams, so the result is a straightforward Government-vs-Opposition decision.
Podium also offers two optional 4-minute Reply Speeches (Opposition Reply, then Government Reply) after the main 6 speeches — a summary-only round used by many tournaments to close out an AP debate.

ld.name: Lincoln-Douglas (LD)
ld.summary: Lincoln-Douglas is a one-on-one debate format focused on values, ethics, and philosophy rather than detailed policy. There are only two debaters — no whip speakers and no closing teams.

duties: Supports the motion (resolution).
Defines key terms if needed.
Presents the value, value criterion, and main arguments.
Defends the case throughout the debate.
responsibilities: Explain why their side best upholds the resolution.

duties: Opposes the motion.
Challenges the Affirmative's framework and arguments.
Presents an alternative value framework and counterarguments.
Explains why the resolution should not be accepted.
responsibilities: Show the resolution is false or should not be accepted.
Undermine the Affirmative's framework and arguments.
Present reasons to reject the resolution.
Demonstrate why their framework is preferable.

ld.speakingOrderNote: Speech times vary slightly depending on the organization (e.g. NSDA, university, or local tournaments). Podium uses this standard 7-stage structure and timing.

qanda.title: Cross-Examination — the Q&A of LD
qanda.explanation: Unlike BP/AP's brief POIs, LD uses two dedicated 3-minute Cross-Examination blocks where one debater directly questions the other in a genuine back-and-forth exchange.
rules: After the Affirmative Constructive: the Negative cross-examines the Affirmative for 3 minutes.
After the Negative Constructive: the Affirmative cross-examines the Negative for 3 minutes.
Cross-examination is used to clarify the opponent's case, expose weaknesses, and set up material for the rebuttal speeches that follow.
In Podium, either side of a cross-ex block can be human (types the question/answer) or AI (generates one automatically) in any combination.

keyConcepts: LD centers on a value (e.g. justice, liberty) and a value criterion (the standard used to weigh that value) rather than a policy proposal.
There are no whip speakers or closing teams — just one Affirmative and one Negative, each speaking for themselves throughout.
The two Cross-Examination blocks are the format's Q&A sessions — direct, timed questioning rather than the brief interjections used in BP/AP.
The Affirmative speaks first and last (AC and 2AR), giving them the final word — balanced by the Negative getting the longest single speech (NC, 7 minutes).
